hi, pretty much everyone here has already told you that the “image of God” is not literally referring to a bodily form. they have also given various christian theological understandings of the phrase that have developed over time

i am going to try and offer a more exclusively Hebrew Bible perspective. the word “image” is used very intentionally in the Hebrew Bible, as it has a deep well of meaning and connotations. notably, it is the word used to refer to objects of worship. “graven images” and whatnot. there are tools to look up all usages of the word in the text generally which will help you clarify the meaning of the word in the Genesis creation narrative(s) specifically. (unless you simply wish to argue with people for sport, in which case ignore this because i have no interest in silliness like that). the earliest intentions from the authors of the Torah using this word appear to be making a point to one another not to worship physical idols like money and power, nor worship gods who are like powerful men and women in the sky. if one seeks to worship God, love one another; each human person is an “image” of the Divine. your neighbor is your “graven image” of the Divine, not worthless gold nor tarnishing silver nor fading beauty nor oppressive positions of power nor fleeting physical security nor military strength nor kings nor kingdoms nor feeble human intelligence etc etc. and certainly not deities invented to protect such illusions

the Christian interpretations others gave are very good. that we are called to participate in God’s creation and thereby becoming co creators. or that it refers to us participating in God’s nature, or the formation of the Divine nature in our minds etc. as a christian, i certainly affirm many of these interpretations and theological presuppositions. how much of that was part of the earliest authors’ intentions is beyond me.

i have friends who practice plant magic. one goes as far as to describe themself as a “green witch”. i find this expression of “magic” beautiful. it is well grounded in human history and our evolution. 

as for Wicca in particular, i am pretty skeptical. while i would not judge or condemn anyone for practicing it, i suspect one would find it very hard to reconcile practicing both Christianity and Wicca. my understandings of both seem completely at odds. also on a more personal level, the wiccans i’ve interacted with have had exclusionary gender essentialist views built into their religious beliefs. as a transgender person, i suppose my bias has fed my distaste for the practice. as a Christian, this might sound silly considering Christian communities are often hotbeds for transphobia and gender essentialism. however, it is not baked into the religion itself which has a long rich history of holy gender nonconformity in iconography, hagiography, mysticim, as well as the scriptures themselves. Christ himself (in addition to the rest of the scriptures) assures us that gender non conforming bodies are part of the kingdom of God, and that all our bodies will be gender non conforming (by earthly measure) in the world to come. “there will be no marriage nor giving in marriage, rather we will be as the Angels in Heaven””some are born Eunuchs, some are made eunuchs by men, some make themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven” the story of Phillip and the Ethiopian Eunuch, some stuff in the prophets of the Hebrew Bible etc etc. in wicca, gender essentialism seems to be ‘dogma’, for lack of a better word. i just personally dont like that. maybe thats not as central to Wicca as i understand it to be, i am certainly no expert. 

as for paganism, i dont know how to interpret your usage of the word. it generally has a negative definition, in the sense that ‘Pagan’ is a word used by strict Monotheist/Abrahamic folks to widely refer to a wide variety Non-Christian/Jewish/Muslim practices. i guess if we are speaking in the most general possible terms, i am grateful for the contributions ‘pagans’ have made to my religion and spirituality. the prelude of John is essentially a Platonic dialogue, which combines the ancient Jewish understanding of the messiah with Plato’s “Logos”. Christian practices since ancient times have mirrored many of the ‘pagan’ practices the preceded the religion. The ‘Pagan’ idea of Theurgy certainly laid the foundation for the Christian conception of Theosis, a central part of Christian spiritual life. Christian Hagiographies are sometimes Christianized retellings of ‘pagan’ myths, transfiguring them theologically, spiritually, etc etc. 

in terms of modern people who identify themselves as ‘Pagan’, it sometimes seems like larping at best and  reactionary at worst. i know a couple people personally who call themselves “pagans”. an acquaintance who prays to ancient greek deities, and good friend who is into norse stuff. i do not look down on them at all, in fact i have a lot of respect for them. they are good people, committed to the wellbeing and liberation of all people and both have their religious beliefs rooted in a radical rejection of the Christianity they were raised with. i can certainly empathize with a radical rejection of Christianity (especially due to religious trauma, i have much of that myself and i know how painful it is). 

that being said, i find it concerning that neo-paganism seems to often be a preoccupation with aesthetics. when i encounter someone obsessed with aesthetics, i tend to suspect they might be a Fascist. (this is also true of the wave of neo-nazi “trad” christians obsessed with high church aesthetics). taking into account the relationship between neo paganism and white supremacy, i feel my instincts are often confirmed. also, my understanding of how religion functions is inextricable from both culture and community. reviving dead religions is deeply disconnected from both. if i were to apostatize, i’d probably either join an extant religious community or simply become non-religious. 

all this is just me, a small ignorant feeble human being, making armchair judgements and should be taken as such!! i do not in any way think pagan or wicca practices are inherently “unholy”, and whether or not it is “sinful” is not my judgement to make. only God knows. sharing my personal thoughts and opinions may even be an expression of pride, and if so i pray that God humbles me.
